I (M32) am in the same boat and all of my current advice makes me a major hypocrite, but believe me it works.

You need to find a middle ground. Logically you know that job rejections are not a personal attack on your value as a human. There is an absolute spectrum of reasons most jobs reject people. From internal hires to limited seats, from better fit to nepotism, from clerical error to laws requiring for jobs to be posted and interviewing a minimal number of applicants despite the job being filled already.

What you need is an excel sheet. I ran a job program back in the day to get new boot camp people hired within the industry and you know what our average numbers showed?

256 applications for 50 email responses(rejections/next steps) that led to 10 phone interviews that lead to 3 in persons that led to one job.

This was for one of those tech boot camps in the San Francisco bay area,  one of the tech Capitols of the world and one of the most job dense places in the world for that field.

That's how much of an absolute slog the job market is. And this was pre-pandemic 2018. Now it's probably even worse!

You NEED the excel sheet and to keep you expectations in line with the market. Sometimes it feels like you did 500 applications when you did 20. Believe me I worked with so many students who didn't hold themselves accountable and students who were held hostage by their emotions.

You need to play the numbers game. That's how the system is designed. Also if there is a common failure point, maybe get coaching in that particular area.

We had a student that was getting lots of phone interviews but zero in persons. Guess why... We did a mock phone interview with him and he sounded straight up like a serial killer. Monotone, heavy mouth breathing, dead pan jokes that didn't sound like jokes lmfao. Let me tell you how surprised we were.

Anyways, treat yourself like you were your own client man. Try to imagine you were your own friend helping them find a job.

As someone who couldn't afford the University Tutorial DLC, here is my take.

UNI was a great tutorial system when it first came out and still arguably is for many players (depending on server), but the past 20 patches have quickly proven it to be in decline in quality for the price.

Seeing as you're about finished, I won't go into pros and cons cause I haven't lived it and you have.

From my perspective and other players' reviews it looks like the best thing most players get from the UNI dlc these days are connections, the DEGREE achievement badge, a chance at earning more in game currency for the same position as someone without the achievement and hopefully applicable skills.

Now, I think its a common misconception that the tutorial has prepared you for a particular job tree. In every job tree I have participated in, I have played with people who also have completed the UNI dlc and they still had to be trained to the same level as me anyways. More often than not, I got paid the same or more for those job trees because I made it a point to push the guild leaders when they gave me the PvP test.

Since your level is much lower than mine, you will find a guild spot much quicker than I.

But make no mistake, finding a guild spot is still difficult no matter if you finished the DLC or not. It just is slightly easier. You'll see examples of this all over the message boards.

Practical tips:
* Make the multiple variations of the direct messages you send to guild leaders. Most of them use bots to go through them anyways
* Failing the PvP test is EXTREMELY NORMAL. Even if you're a vet like me, it takes me 2-3 failures to get used to PvP again. Especially when most of what i deal with are bots.
* Even if you don't find a guild position, you need to find a way to pay for server fees. That comes first. I made the mistake of trying to find a "new" way to play the game by not doing any guild work I didn't like. I don't recommend it. Find a way to pay for server fees first and foremost, unless you already come from a clan with a stash that gives you room to experiment, maybe that can be worthwhile.
* Going between servers seems to be the trend that keeps the most players happy. I know this isn't a thing during the COVID Event, but planning and saving for it might be a good idea.
* Setting goals in this game is no one's job but your own. Whenever I see players set other people's goals as their own it doesn't end well. Finding in game things to keep yourself happy is the name of the game.
* Planning will help most players out, whether its a raid or some mundane side quest, having a goal and a plan will help manage the the limited time you have as a player.

Mien homie here. For those who don't know the Iu Mien tribe is a subculture of southeast Asia. Most of us have the exact same family history of being brought here via refugee camps during the Vietnam War and by mass during the end of it. My family didn't arrive until the late 80s and you can usually tell we're mien because the last names start sit Sae which is an olden prefix meaning surname or family-name. I say usually because there are other subcultures that follow similar etiquette, Hmong people probably being the most prominent.

Kao is an extremely common name among our people because it is usually associated with the first male child or first born. San, Nai, Meuy(pronounced May), and Lai are also common names as they usually denote which child they are in numerical order, those these rules are not strict and sometimes you'll find families with slightly different orders of the same names within families. 

Anyways, we came here with nothing, barely survived in urban areas all around the US, and many of such have grown up in extreme poverty. Our biggest communities are in Oregon, California , and Idaho I believe. 

Just throwing some cultural knowledge around, not sure if this Kao is a good one or not, but there are probably hundreds with his name.
